lead: Bars come in stock lengths of about 12 m, so long members need joints; the usual joint is a lap splice, two bars overlapped so the force passes from one to the other through the concrete. Bars are also stopped (curtailed) where the bending moment has fallen enough for fewer bars to do the work. Both are safe only if every bar has its development length and the joints and cut-offs are placed where the code allows. Only a few syllabi list this as a separate topic, but every detailing question uses it.
prereq: You need: Ld and the anchorage values of hooks from Bond, anchorage and development length, and the moment of resistance of a beam section (limit state design of beams).

items: Flexural tension: lap length = the greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. Direct tension (ties): the greater of 2 L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. The straight length of a lap must be at least 15φ or 200 mm.
Compression: lap length = L<sub>d</sub> in compression, but not less than 24φ.

Increase the tension lap by 1.4 for a bar at the top of a section as cast with cover less than 2φ, or at a corner with cover less than 2φ, or where adjacent laps are closer than 75 mm or 6φ; by 2.0 when both conditions apply.
Bars of different diameters: the lap length is based on the smaller bar, because the joint can never pass more force than the smaller bar carries.
Laps are not used for bars larger than 36 mm; such bars are welded or joined with mechanical couplers.

blocks.text: Place laps away from the sections of maximum stress: in a flexural member, not where the moment is more than half the moment of resistance. Splice not more than half the bars at one section, and stagger the laps; laps count as staggered when their centres are at least 1.3 times the lap length apart. Bunched laps make one weak, crowded section that cracks first and is hard to concrete. Some syllabi call this topic 'splicing of reinforcement'.

Plot the moment diagram and the moment of resistance M<sub>R</sub> of the bars that continue. The theoretical cut-off point of the stopped bars is where the moment falls to that M<sub>R</sub>: beyond it they are not needed for flexure. They cannot stop there, because an inclined crack starting there shifts the bar force towards the support.

items: Extend every curtailed bar beyond its theoretical cut-off by the greater of d and 12φ (not needed at a simple support or at the free end of a cantilever).
Every bar must also have L<sub>d</sub> measured from the section where it is fully stressed, and the continuing bars must have L<sub>d</sub> beyond the theoretical cut-off.

A bar should not stop in a tension zone unless one of three conditions holds: the shear at the cut-off is not more than two thirds of the shear capacity including the stirrups; or extra stirrups are provided over 0.75 d from the cut-off; or, for bars up to 36 mm, the continuing bars give twice the area needed there and the shear is not more than three quarters of the capacity.
At a simple support at least one third of the positive steel (one quarter in a continuous beam) runs into the support for L<sub>d</sub>/3.
At a continuous support at least one third of the negative steel runs beyond the point of inflection by the greatest of d, 12φ and one sixteenth of the clear span.

examples.question: A simply supported beam of 6 m effective span, b = 300 mm, d = 450 mm (M25, Fe415), has four 16 mm bars at midspan and carries a uniform factored load giving M<sub>u</sub> = 110 kN·m at midspan. Two bars are to be curtailed and two continued to the supports. Find the theoretical and the actual cut-off points and check the shear condition, with two-legged 8 mm stirrups at 300 mm.
steps: Load: w<sub>u</sub> = 8 M<sub>u</sub>/L² = 8 × 110/36 = 24.44 kN/m, and M(x) = 110 × 4x(6 − x)/36 at x m from a support.
Theoretical cut-off: 110 × 4x(6 − x)/36 = 62.1 gives x² − 6x + 5.08 = 0, so x = (6 − √(36 − 20.32))/2 = 1.02 m from each support.
Extension: the greater of d = 450 mm and 12φ = 192 mm, so 450 mm. Actual cut-off at 1.02 − 0.45 = 0.57 m from each support; the curtailed bars run from 0.57 m to 5.43 m.

Development length: L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm. The curtailed bars are fully stressed at midspan and have 3.00 − 0.57 = 2.43 m beyond it, more than 645 mm. The continuing bars have 1.02 m plus their anchorage beyond the theoretical cut-off, also more than 645 mm.
Two thirds of the capacity = 70.9 kN ≥ 59.4 kN, so the bars may stop in the tension zone with no extra stirrups.
examples.answer: Theoretical cut-off 1.02 m from each support; actual cut-off 0.57 m (extension d = 450 mm). The shear there, 59.4 kN, is below two thirds of the capacity, 70.9 kN, so the curtailment is allowed.

examples.question: For the same beam (M25, Fe415, 16 mm bars, L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm), find (a) the lap length of a bottom bar lapped in flexural tension, (b) the lap of a top bar with 25 mm cover, (c) the minimum centre-to-centre distance for the laps of (a) to count as staggered, and (d) the lap of a 16 mm column bar in compression.
steps: (a) Greater of L<sub>d</sub> = 645 mm and 30φ = 480 mm: 645 mm, provide 650 mm.
(b) Top bar as cast with cover 25 mm < 2φ = 32 mm: 1.4 × 650 = 910 mm.
(d) Compression: L<sub>d</sub> = 16 × 361.05/(4 × 2.80) = 516 mm; 24φ = 384 mm; provide 520 mm.
examples.answer: 650 mm in flexural tension, 910 mm for the top bar, laps staggered at 845 mm or more, and 520 mm in compression.

traps: Stopping bars at the theoretical cut-off. They must run on by the greater of d and 12φ: 450 mm in the worked example, not 192 mm.
Basing the lap of bars of two diameters on the larger bar. IS 456 bases it on the smaller bar.
Forgetting the 30φ minimum in tension or the 24φ minimum in compression, or the factor 1.4 for top bars with thin cover.
Lapping all bars at one section, or at the section of maximum moment.
Curtailing in a tension zone without checking the shear at the cut-off against two thirds of the capacity.

quiz.q: State the lap length in flexural tension and in direct tension.
quiz.a: Flexural tension: the greater of L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ. Direct tension: the greater of 2 L<sub>d</sub> and 30φ.

quiz.q: Why must a bar run past its theoretical cut-off point?
quiz.a: An inclined crack starting near the cut-off carries the bar force further towards the support than the moment diagram shows, and the moment diagram itself is uncertain. The extension of d or 12φ covers this shift.

quiz.q: A 20 mm Fe415 bar in M25 has L<sub>d</sub> = 806 mm. Find its lap in flexural tension and in direct tension.
quiz.a: Flexural: greater of 806 and 30 × 20 = 600 mm, so 806 mm, say 810 mm. Direct tension: greater of 2 × 806 = 1612 and 600 mm, so 1612 mm, say 1620 mm.

quiz.q: A 16 mm bar is lapped with a 20 mm bar in flexural tension (M25, Fe415). Find the lap length.
quiz.a: Based on the smaller bar: greater of 645 mm and 30 × 16 = 480 mm, so 645 mm, say 650 mm.

A lapped section has twice the steel in a short length and depends on bond between the two bars, so it is crowded and cracks first. If all bars lap at one section that weakness affects the whole section; staggering spreads it so most bars are continuous at any section.

quiz.q: In worked example 1, the stirrups were at 450 mm instead of 300 mm. Would the curtailment still be allowed?
quiz.a: 450 mm exceeds the 0.75 d = 337.5 mm limit, so the layout is not allowed anyway. Even ignoring that, stirrups at 450 mm carry 36.3 kN; the capacity is 52.0 + 36.3 = 88.3 kN and two thirds is 58.9 kN, below the 59.4 kN shear, so extra stirrups would be needed at the cut-off.

beyond: Not for the exam. Site teams use mechanical couplers (threaded or swaged sleeves) for large bars and in congested columns, and earthquake codes such as IS 13920 forbid laps in plastic hinge zones and demand closely spaced hoops over any lap. Bar bending software now optimises cut lengths to reduce waste from 12 m stock bars. Search for 'mechanical splices for reinforcement', 'IS 13920 lap splice rules' and 'rebar cutting optimisation'.
